demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 78-year-old retired environmental scientist, a man whose life was once defined by precision, measurement, and the slow, careful work of restoring damaged ecosystems. He sits in the chair across from me with his hands folded in his lap, his posture rigid, as if he is bracing for impact. He speaks softly, with a formal politeness that feels like a barrier. He has been married to his wife, Leila, for fifty-two years. He tells me, with a hollow laugh, that she is the one who finally made him come here. "She says I am not myself," he explains, his eyes fixed on a spot on the floor. "She is right. I do not know who I am anymore."

The story he tells begins on a Tuesday morning, fourteen months ago. He was in the final year of a major project-a remediation plan for a coastal wetland that had been poisoned by industrial runoff. It was his magnum opus, the culmination of a long career. He was driving to a field site on a narrow, winding road that hugged the edge of a salt marsh. He remembers the light, the way it glinted off the water. He remembers the smell of brine and wet earth. He was thinking about a data point, a salinity reading that didn't fit the model.

Then, it happened.

A young man, a graduate student named Samir, was cycling on the shoulder. Mr. A. does not remember if he swerved, or if the cyclist did. He does not remember a sound of impact. He only remembers the silence after, and the terrible stillness of the bicycle wheel, still spinning, catching the sun. He got out of his car. Samir was lying on the ground, his leg bent at an impossible angle, a dark pool of blood spreading on the asphalt. Mr. A. held the boy's head, trying to keep him still, telling him help was coming. He remembers the feel of the young man's hair, damp with sweat and blood.

Samir survived, but his leg was shattered. He underwent multiple surgeries and will walk with a permanent limp. The police report concluded it was a tragic accident; no charges were filed. The insurance companies handled the rest.

But for Mr. A., the accident did not end. It is happening still, every single day.

He cannot drive anymore. The mere sight of a bicycle, even one locked to a rack, makes his heart pound so hard he feels he might faint. He has stopped going to the grocery store because the parking lot is full of cars, and he is terrified of pulling out, of not seeing someone, of causing another catastrophe. He spends most of his days in his home office, surrounded by old maps and soil samples. He tries to read scientific journals, but the words blur. He finds himself staring at a single page for an hour, his mind replaying the image of the spinning wheel.

He has nightmares, but they are not the typical replays of the crash. In his dreams, he is in a vast, sterile laboratory. He is measuring something, pouring a liquid from one beaker to another. But the liquid is blood, and it keeps overflowing, spilling onto the white floor. He wakes up gasping, covered in sweat, and cannot go back to sleep. He is exhausted, a deep, bone-weariness that coffee cannot touch.

The guilt is a physical weight in his chest. He, the man who spent decades calculating the precise impact of a molecule on an ecosystem, who believed in the power of data to predict and prevent harm, now lives with an outcome he cannot reverse. He tells me he does not deserve peace. He has stopped attending his weekly bird-watching group. The sight of the herons and egrets, which once filled him with a quiet joy, now only reminds him of the fragile, injured body on the road.

He is irritable with Leila, snapping at her for small things, then retreating into a cold silence. He feels disconnected from her, from his children, from the world. He feels like he is living behind a sheet of thick glass. He can see life happening, but he cannot feel it. "I was a scientist," he says, finally looking up at me. "I believed in cause and effect. I caused this effect. And I cannot find a way to live with it."
